name_zh: 奥凯蒂茶园大吉岭红茶
processing: Made as Darjeeling orthodox tea, typically withered, rolled, oxidised and fired; first flush lots are usually oxidised more lightly than summer ones. Details vary by lot.
harvest_season: As across Darjeeling, picking runs from spring into autumn, with first flush in spring and second flush in early summer as the best-known lots.
appearance_dry: Typically a mix of olive-brown and darker twisted leaf with some silver tips, greener in spring lots and browner in summer ones.
appearance_liquor: Bright pale gold to amber, deeper in summer and autumn lots.
appearance_wet: Mixed green and copper leaf, as is usual for orthodox Darjeeling.
taste_profile: Little is recorded about this garden's cup in particular. Typical of Darjeeling, expect a light floral brightness in spring lots and more fruit and body in summer ones.

brewing.notes: Usually brewed Western-style. Use slightly cooler water and a shorter steep for spring lots, since they turn sharp when pushed.

vintage_note: Sold by year and flush, like other estate Darjeelings, with the invoice or lot often named. Spring and summer lots of the current year are the norm, and fresher is better for first flush.
description:
Okayti is a Darjeeling garden in the Mirik Valley, about 45 km from Darjeeling town, with Gopaldhara and Thurbo as neighbours. Its bushes grow between roughly 1,200 and 1,900 metres, and its name is one of the better stories in the district.

About 209 hectares of its 647 are under tea, the rest largely forest. As with other Darjeeling gardens, what ends up in the bag depends heavily on the season: spring leaf is handled gently and stays green, while later pickings go further toward a true black tea.

The character of this garden's cup is not well documented, so treat flush as your first guide. Typical of Darjeeling, spring tea is light and floral and summer tea is rounder and fruitier. Steep gently at first and taste before adding time.

Most of the roughly 140,000 kg made each year is exported to the US, Europe and Japan, so you will mostly meet it through foreign retailers. Look for a stated year and flush, and be wary of a garden name with neither.
history:
The garden was planted by British planters in the 1870s under the name Rangdoo. Its tea reportedly earned a name in the market as the only "okay tea", and the estate was renamed Okayti after that; this is the usual account, and it is hard to test. The factory dates from 1888.

The estate has more recently been acquired by Rajeev Baid, founder of the Evergreen Group.
